newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX gasoline ends sharply up on short covering.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX gasoline ends sharply up on short covering.

text.p: NYMEX refined product prices rallied sharply Thursday for the second consecutive session, with gasoline beginning to outpace heating oil's gains on short covering ahead of the February contract expiry.

"Clearly it was a products oriented day. You had a lot of the upside coming from short covering in February with the market just shrugging off bearish news," said Gerald Samuels, managing director at ARB Oil.
Feb heating oil settled 1.50 cents higher at 70.34 cents a gallon while Feb gasoline ended up 1.59 cents at 69.82 cents a gallon.
"It was all short covering in gasoline which just accelerated after buy stops were triggered at around 69.10 and 69.20," said a New York gasoline dealer about gasoline's increased momentum.
March crude finished 40 cents higher at $24.87 a barrel despite news the U.N. Secretary General said he expected the oil-for-food deal with Iraq to be renewed another six months in June.
On Thursday, U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan, speaking to a news conference in Geneva, said of the U.N. oil-for-food deal with Iraq:
"My expectation is now that we are beginning the scheme, it will continue to be extended another six months."

Last December, the United Nations eased sanctions against Iraq and enabled Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil every six months, on a renewable basis, in exchange for humanitarian aid. The U.N. sanctions were imposed following Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

Countering the prospect of increased crude supply from Iraq was news that two of Mexico's largest crude ports remained shut for a third day on Thursday as a cold front continued to bring winds of about 50 km per hour to the area, port officials said.
The closed ports of Pajaritos and Dos Bocas each export 399,000 barrels per day (bpd) and 440,000 bpd respectively.

Meanwhile, sideways trading activity in the past two weeks has resulted in an increase in short positions in gasoline and particularly in heating oil, dealers said. Heat historically declines in January.
"Usually heating oil gets killed in January, but it's not happening this time around, so a lot traders have to cover" said a dealer.

A spate of seasonal refinery maintenance is diminishing heating oil and gasoline output, creating some prompt supply tightness and thereby some concern of a short squeeze ahead of the February contract expiry, traders said. Moreover, weather forecasters expected strong demand for heat near term.
The National Weather Service's six to 10 day forecast starting February 4 called for below normal temperatures in much of the key heating oil market of the northeastern United States.
((-- Harry Milling, New York Energy Desk, 212-859-1761))
